cards.title: Format license keys
cards.question:
Remove existing dashes from an alphanumeric key and uppercase its letters. Insert separators so groups counted from the right have size k, allowing only the first group to be shorter.

Official problem and judge on LeetCode ↗
cards.answer:
Overview

Test Cases

key="ab-12-cd-3", k=3 → "A-B12-CD3"

Also check empty inputs and boundary sizes. The JavaScript companion includes runnable assertions.

Constraints

  • Is the output a string?
    • Yes
  • Can we change the input string?
    • No, you can't modify the input string
  • Can we assume the inputs are valid?
    • No
  • Can we assume this fits memory?
    • Yes

Algorithm

  • Loop through each character in the license key backwards, keeping a count of the number of chars we've reached so far, while inserting each character into a result list (convert to upper case)
    • If we reach a '-', skip it
    • Whenever we reach a char count of k, append a '-' character to the result list, reset the char count
  • Careful that we don't have a leading '-', which we might hit with test case: '2-4A0r7-4k', k=4 -> '24A0-R74K'
  • Reverse the result list and return it

Complexity:

  • Time: O(n)
  • Space: O(n)

Code

class Solution(object):

    def format_license_key(self, license_key, k):
        if not isinstance(license_key, str):
            raise TypeError('license_key must be a str')
        if not isinstance(k, int):
            raise TypeError('k must be an int')
        if not license_key:
            raise ValueError('license_key must not be empty')
        formatted_license_key = []
        num_chars = 0
        for char in license_key[::-1]:
            if char == '-':
                continue
            num_chars += 1
            formatted_license_key.append(char.upper())
            if num_chars >= k:
                formatted_license_key.append('-')
                num_chars = 0
        if formatted_license_key and formatted_license_key[-1] == '-':
            formatted_license_key.pop(-1)
        return ''.join(formatted_license_key[::-1])

cards.title: Find the busiest period
cards.question: Problem: Given an array of (unix_timestamp, num_people, EventType.ENTER or EventType.EXIT), find the busiest period.
cards.answer:
Constraints

  • Can we assume the input array is valid?
    • Check for None
  • Can we assume the elements of the input array are valid?
    • Yes
  • Is the input sorted by time?
    • No
  • Can you have enter and exit elements for the same timestamp?
    • Yes you can, order of enter and exit is not guaranteed
  • Could we have multiple enter events (or multiple exit events) for the same timestamp?
    • No
  • What is the format of the output?
    • An array of timestamps [t1, t2]
  • Can we assume the starting number of people is zero?
    • Yes
  • Can we assume the inputs are valid?
    • No
  • Can we assume this fits memory?
    • Yes

Test Cases

  • None -> TypeError
  • [] -> None
  • General case
timestamp  num_people  event_type
3          2           EventType.EXIT
1          2           EventType.ENTER
3          1           EventType.ENTER
7          3           EventType.ENTER
9          2           EventType.EXIT
8          2           EventType.EXIT

result = Period(7, 8)

Algorithm

Since the input is not sorted, we'll need to sort it first by timestamp, ascending.

For each interval in the data set:

  • If this is an "enter" event, increment curr_people, else, decrement
  • Since we can have an "enter" and "exit" event for the same timestamp, we'll need to look ahead one
    • If the next element has the same timestamp, hold off (continue) on updating max_people and max_period
    • Watch out for indexing out-of-bounds at the end of the array
  • Update max_people and max_period

Sorted:

timestamp  num_people  event_type       curr_people  max_people       max_period
1          2           EventType.ENTER  2            2                [1, 3]
3          1           EventType.ENTER  3            2 (not updated)  [1, 3]
3          2           EventType.EXIT   1            2                [3, 7]
7          3           EventType.ENTER  4            4                [7, 8]
8          2           EventType.EXIT   2            4                [7, 8]
9          2           EventType.EXIT   0            4                [7, 8]

Complexity:

  • Time: O(nlog(n)) for the sort
  • Space: O(1), assuming the sort is in-place

Code

from enum import Enum


class Data(object):

    def __init__(self, timestamp, num_people, event_type):
        self.timestamp = timestamp
        self.num_people = num_people
        self.event_type = event_type

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.timestamp < other.timestamp


class Period(object):

    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.start == other.start and self.end == other.end

    def __repr__(self):
        return str(self.start) + ', ' + str(self.end)


class EventType(Enum):

    ENTER = 0
    EXIT = 1



class Solution(object):

    def find_busiest_period(self, data):
        if data is None:
            raise TypeError('data cannot be None')
        if not data:
            return None
        data.sort()
        max_period = Period(0, 0)
        max_people = 0
        curr_people = 0
        for index, interval in enumerate(data):
            if interval.event_type == EventType.ENTER:
                curr_people += interval.num_people
            elif interval.event_type == EventType.EXIT:
                curr_people -= interval.num_people
            else:
                raise ValueError('Invalid event type')
            if (index < len(data) - 1 and
                    data[index].timestamp == data[index + 1].timestamp):
                continue
            if curr_people > max_people:
                max_people = curr_people
                max_period.start = data[index].timestamp
                if index < len(data) - 1:
                    max_period.end = data[index + 1].timestamp
                else:
                    max_period.end = data[index].timestamp
        return max_period

Unit Test

%%writefile test_find_busiest_period.py
from nose.tools import assert_equal, assert_raises


class TestSolution(object):

    def test_find_busiest_period(self):
        solution = Solution()
        assert_raises(TypeError, solution.find_busiest_period, None)
        assert_equal(solution.find_busiest_period([]), None)
        data = [
            Data(3, 2, EventType.EXIT),
            Data(1, 2, EventType.ENTER),
            Data(3, 1, EventType.ENTER),
            Data(7, 3, EventType.ENTER),
            Data(9, 2, EventType.EXIT),
            Data(8, 2, EventType.EXIT),
        ]
        assert_equal(solution.find_busiest_period(data), Period(7, 8))
        print('Success: test_find_busiest_period')


def main():
    test = TestSolution()
    test.test_find_busiest_period()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

cards.title: Build a min heap
cards.question: Problem: Implement a min heap with extract_min and insert methods.
cards.answer:
Constraints

  • Can we assume the inputs are ints?
    • Yes
  • Can we assume this fits memory?
    • Yes

Test Cases

  • Extract min of an empty tree
  • Extract min general case
  • Insert into an empty tree
  • Insert general case (left and right insert)
          _5_
        /     \
       20     15
      / \    /  \
     22  40 25

extract_min(): 5

          _15_
        /      \
       20      25
      / \     /  \
     22  40

insert(2):

          _2_
        /     \
       20      5
      / \     / \
     22  40  25  15

Algorithm

A heap is a complete binary tree where each node is smaller than its children.

extract_min

          _5_
        /     \
       20     15
      / \    /  \
     22  40 25

Save the root as the value to be returned: 5
Move the right most element to the root: 25

          _25_
        /      \
       20      15
      / \     /  \
     22  40

Bubble down 25: Swap 25 and 15 (the smaller child)

          _15_
        /      \
       20      25
      / \     /  \
     22  40

Return 5

We'll use an array to represent the tree, here are the indices:

          _0_
        /     \
       1       2
      / \     / \
     3   4

To get to a child, we take 2 index + 1 (left child) or 2 index + 2 (right child).

For example, the right child of index 1 is 2 * 1 + 2 = 4.

Complexity:

  • Time: O(lg(n))
  • Space: O(lg(n)) for the recursion depth (tree height), or O(1) if using an iterative approach

insert

          _5_
        /     \
       20     15
      / \    /  \
     22  40 25

insert(2):
Insert at the right-most spot to maintain the heap property.

          _5_
        /     \
       20     15
      / \    /  \
     22  40 25   2

Bubble up 2: Swap 2 and 15

          _5_
        /     \
       20     2
      / \    / \
     22  40 25  15

Bubble up 2: Swap 2 and 5

          _2_
        /     \
       20     5
      / \    / \
     22  40 25  15

We'll use an array to represent the tree, here are the indices:

          _0_
        /     \
       1       2
      / \     / \
     3   4   5   6

To get to a parent, we take (index - 1) // 2.

For example, the parent of index 6 is (6 - 1) // 2 = 2.

Complexity:

  • Time: O(lg(n))
  • Space: O(lg(n)) for the recursion depth (tree height), or O(1) if using an iterative approach

Code

%%writefile min_heap.py
from __future__ import division

import sys


class MinHeap(object):

    def __init__(self):
        self.array = []

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.array)

    def extract_min(self):
        if not self.array:
            return None
        if len(self.array) == 1:
            return self.array.pop(0)
        minimum = self.array[0]
        # Move the last element to the root
        self.array[0] = self.array.pop(-1)
        self._bubble_down(index=0)
        return minimum

    def peek_min(self):
        return self.array[0] if self.array else None

    def insert(self, key):
        if key is None:
            raise TypeError('key cannot be None')
        self.array.append(key)
        self._bubble_up(index=len(self.array) - 1)

    def _bubble_up(self, index):
        if index == 0:
            return
        index_parent = (index - 1) // 2
        if self.array[index] < self.array[index_parent]:
            # Swap the indices and recurse
            self.array[index], self.array[index_parent] = \
                self.array[index_parent], self.array[index]
            self._bubble_up(index_parent)

    def _bubble_down(self, index):
        min_child_index = self._find_smaller_child(index)
        if min_child_index == -1:
            return
        if self.array[index] > self.array[min_child_index]:
            # Swap the indices and recurse
            self.array[index], self.array[min_child_index] = \
                self.array[min_child_index], self.array[index]
            self._bubble_down(min_child_index)

    def _find_smaller_child(self, index):
        left_child_index = 2 * index + 1
        right_child_index = 2 * index + 2
        # No right child
        if right_child_index >= len(self.array):
            # No left child

%%writefile min_heap.py
from __future__ import division

import sys


class MinHeap(object):

    def __init__(self):
        self.array = []

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.array)

    def extract_min(self):
        if not self.array:
            return None
        if len(self.array) == 1:
            return self.array.pop(0)
        minimum = self.array[0]
        # Move the last element to the root
        self.array[0] = self.array.pop(-1)
        self._bubble_down(index=0)
        return minimum

    def peek_min(self):
        return self.array[0] if self.array else None

    def insert(self, key):
        if key is None:
            raise TypeError('key cannot be None')
        self.array.append(key)
        self._bubble_up(index=len(self.array) - 1)

    def _bubble_up(self, index):
        if index == 0:
            return
        index_parent = (index - 1) // 2
        if self.array[index] < self.array[index_parent]:
            # Swap the indices and recurse
            self.array[index], self.array[index_parent] = \
                self.array[index_parent], self.array[index]
            self._bubble_up(index_parent)

    def _bubble_down(self, index):
        min_child_index = self._find_smaller_child(index)
        if min_child_index == -1:
            return
        if self.array[index] > self.array[min_child_index]:
            # Swap the indices and recurse
            self.array[index], self.array[min_child_index] = \
                self.array[min_child_index], self.array[index]
            self._bubble_down(min_child_index)

    def _find_smaller_child(self, index):
        left_child_index = 2 * index + 1
        right_child_index = 2 * index + 2
        # No right child
        if right_child_index >= len(self.array):
            # No left child
            if left_child_index >= len(self.array):
                return -1
            # Left child only
            else:
                return left_child_index
        else:
            # Compare left and right children
            if self.array[left_child_index] < self.array[right_child_index]:
                return left_child_index
            else:
                return right_child_index

cards.title: Performance vs scalability
cards.question: Explain performance vs scalability and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Performance describes how much work a system completes and how quickly it responds at a particular load. Scalability describes how those measurements change as traffic, data, or available resources grow.

Design considerations

Measure a baseline, identify the limiting resource, and repeat the measurement at higher load. Adding servers helps only if the constrained work can be distributed; a shared database or serialized operation may remain the bottleneck.

cards.title: Latency vs throughput
cards.question: Explain latency vs throughput and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Latency measures elapsed time for an operation. Throughput measures completed operations per unit of time. Parallel work can raise throughput without reducing the latency of any individual request.

Design considerations

Track percentiles as well as averages. Near saturation, queues grow and tail latency can rise sharply. Use load tests that include bursts and slow dependencies; bound queues and shed work before deadlines become meaningless.

cards.title: Consistency patterns
cards.question: Explain consistency patterns and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Consistency describes which versions of data an operation may observe. Linearizable operations behave as if each took effect at one instant between invocation and completion. Eventual convergence permits temporary disagreement between replicas.

Design considerations

Choose guarantees per workflow. Read-your-writes can make a user’s own updates immediately visible without promising global linearizability. State what happens during replication lag, conflicts, failover, and retries rather than relying only on a label such as “strong.”

cards.title: Availability patterns
cards.question: Explain availability patterns and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Replication and failover can keep a service usable when components fail. In an active-passive setup, a standby takes over; in an active-active setup, multiple instances already accept work.

Design considerations

Define failure detection, leader fencing, and recovery procedures. A standby must have sufficient capacity and sufficiently fresh state. Active-active writes require conflict handling or partitioned ownership. Test failover under load and track recovery time and possible data loss.

cards.title: Availability vs consistency
cards.question: Explain availability vs consistency and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

During a network partition, a distributed service cannot always both return a successful response to every request at a non-failing node and preserve linearizable behavior. The CAP terms describe a specific failure model.

Design considerations

For each operation, decide whether to reject or delay requests, serve possibly stale data, or accept writes that need reconciliation. Real designs can make different choices for inventory changes and catalog browsing. CAP availability is not the same measurement as a monthly uptime percentage.

cards.title: Domain name system
cards.question: Explain domain name system and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

DNS resolves names through a hierarchy of authoritative servers and caches. A client usually asks a recursive resolver, which obtains an answer and can reuse it until its time-to-live expires.

Design considerations

DNS caching reduces lookup traffic but makes changes gradual. Plan for stale addresses, negative caching, and resolver behavior. DNS-based traffic steering is relatively coarse; application health and request-level routing often need a load balancer as well.

cards.question: Explain content delivery network and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A CDN serves eligible content from locations closer to clients. Cacheable responses can avoid an origin round trip, reducing latency and origin traffic. A cache key determines which requests may share a stored response.

Design considerations

Define cache keys, freshness, invalidation, and treatment of personalized content. Versioned asset URLs simplify long-lived caching. Protect the origin from a flood of simultaneous misses and confirm that private responses cannot be served to another user.

cards.title: Load balancer
cards.question: Explain load balancer and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A load balancer distributes traffic among healthy backends. Transport-level routing handles connections, while application-level routing can inspect HTTP paths, headers, and other request information.

Design considerations

Choose a balancing policy that reflects backend capacity and request cost. Use health checks, graceful draining, bounded retries, and timeouts. Session affinity can ease stateful designs but complicates failover; shared or client-carried session state often improves flexibility.

cards.title: Reverse proxy (web server)
cards.question: Explain reverse proxy (web server) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A reverse proxy accepts requests on behalf of origin servers. It can terminate TLS, route requests, enforce limits, compress responses, or cache content. Load balancing is one capability a reverse proxy may provide.

Design considerations

Configure trusted forwarding headers carefully, and distinguish the client address from the proxy connection address. Match upstream timeouts to the request budget. Keep sensitive routes and cached responses isolated, and avoid making the proxy a single point of failure.

cards.title: Application layer
cards.question: Explain application layer and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

The application layer implements business operations and coordinates storage and other services. Keeping request handlers free of local durable state makes it easier to add instances and replace failed ones.

Design considerations

Separate responsibilities when the boundary improves ownership, scaling, or reliability. Every network boundary also introduces latency and partial failures. Use explicit contracts, deadlines, tracing, and idempotency when requests cross those boundaries.

cards.title: Database
cards.question: Explain database and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A database manages persistent state and the rules for reading and changing it. Indexes, transactions, replication, and recovery mechanisms address different needs; none removes the need to understand the access pattern.

Design considerations

Start with data size, read/write rates, transaction boundaries, and required queries. Measure query plans and contention before adding replicas or shards. Backups need restore tests, and replication alone is not a backup against accidental deletion.

cards.title: Federation
cards.question: Explain federation and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Functional partitioning separates different domains into separate databases or services, such as accounts, billing, and catalog data. Each domain can then be operated and scaled with more independence.

Design considerations

Cross-domain queries and transactions become harder. Prefer stable ownership boundaries and explicit integration contracts. Decide how to propagate updates, repair failed workflows, and produce reports without recreating tight coupling through synchronous calls.

cards.title: Sharding
cards.question: Explain sharding and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Sharding divides one logical dataset across storage nodes. A shard key determines where each record belongs. Range partitioning preserves locality; hashing usually spreads keys more evenly but makes range scans harder.

Design considerations

Evaluate hot keys, growth, cross-shard queries, and rebalancing. A uniformly distributed key is not enough if a small set of records receives most traffic. Record ownership and migration need a clear protocol so reads and writes remain correct while data moves.

cards.title: Denormalization
cards.question: Explain denormalization and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Denormalization stores a value or relationship in more than one place to reduce expensive reads or joins. Materialized views and precomputed aggregates are common examples.

Design considerations

Treat duplicated data as a maintained projection with a source of truth. Define update ordering, freshness requirements, backfills, and reconciliation. Compare saved read cost with extra writes, storage, and the operational burden of repairing divergence.

cards.title: SQL tuning
cards.question: Explain sql tuning and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Tune SQL from observed slow queries and execution plans. Examine scanned rows, indexes, join strategies, sorting, lock waits, and how much data is returned. An index can accelerate reads while increasing write and storage costs.

Design considerations

Use representative data and parameter distributions. Avoid fetching unused columns and repeated per-row queries. Check pagination, transaction length, and connection-pool limits. Re-measure after each change; an optimization for one workload may hurt another.

cards.title: NoSQL
cards.question: Explain nosql and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

NoSQL is a broad category containing key-value, document, wide-column, and graph databases. These systems make different choices about queries, schemas, transactions, and distribution. The category alone does not imply one consistency model.

Design considerations

Select a concrete database by its documented guarantees and your access patterns. Ask about atomic updates, indexes, backup/restore, failure behavior, and operating cost. A flexible record shape still needs application-level validation and migration planning.

cards.title: Key-value store
cards.question: Explain key-value store and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A key-value store retrieves a value by an identifier. The value may be opaque to the storage engine or support limited server-side operations. This model suits lookups such as sessions, counters, and cached objects.

Design considerations

Determine key size, value size, expiration, and atomic-operation needs. Design for hot keys and large values. Queries that require scanning many keys or filtering inside values may need an additional index or a different storage model.

cards.title: Document store
cards.question: Explain document store and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A document database stores records with nested fields, often with indexes over selected paths. Keeping related data in one document can make reads convenient and make some updates atomic within that document.

Design considerations

Decide what to embed and what to reference. Watch document growth, duplicated values, and index cost. Flexible schemas can coexist across versions, so readers and writers need explicit compatibility rules. Transaction guarantees depend on the specific database.

cards.title: Wide column store
cards.question: Explain wide column store and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A wide-column model organizes data around partition keys and ordered rows or columns within a partition. Query design commonly starts from the operations that must be efficient, then shapes tables around those operations.

Design considerations

Choose bounded partitions and avoid concentrating writes on one partition. Understand compaction, retention, and tombstone behavior. Joins and arbitrary filters may be expensive or unavailable, so another table or projection can be needed for a different query pattern.

cards.title: Graph database
cards.question: Explain graph database and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A graph model represents entities as vertices and relationships as edges. It is useful when traversing connections is central to the workload, such as finding related entities or exploring paths.

Design considerations

Estimate traversal depth, fan-out, and filtering selectivity. An unbounded traversal can still be expensive. Clarify relationship direction, transaction requirements, and whether the graph fits on one node; partitioning highly connected data can introduce substantial cross-node work.

cards.title: SQL or NoSQL
cards.question: Explain sql or nosql and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Choose a storage system from required operations and guarantees, rather than from a category slogan. Relational databases are often a strong default when relationships, constraints, and flexible queries matter. Specialized stores can suit particular access patterns.

Design considerations

Write down transaction scope, latency goals, data volume, growth, consistency, and operational skills. Prototype representative queries and failure recovery. Multiple stores can help, but each additional system introduces synchronization and ownership costs.

cards.title: Cache
cards.question: Explain cache and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

A cache keeps a reusable result closer to its consumers or in a faster storage tier. A hit avoids some underlying work; a miss still pays the retrieval or computation cost, plus cache overhead.

Design considerations

Define the cache key, freshness policy, size bound, and eviction strategy. Measure hit rate and latency by request class. Plan for stampedes, hot keys, stale data, and total cache loss; the backing service must not collapse when the cache restarts.

cards.title: Cache locations
cards.question: Explain cache locations and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Caching can happen in browsers, a CDN, reverse proxies, application memory, shared cache services, or database internals. Each location saves a different part of the request path and has a different scope.

Design considerations

Local caches avoid network calls but duplicate memory and complicate invalidation across instances. Shared caches coordinate better but add a dependency. Place sensitive or personalized data only where the cache key and access controls preserve isolation.

cards.title: Database caching, what to cache
cards.question: Explain database caching, what to cache and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Good cache candidates are repeatedly read results whose retrieval is expensive and whose freshness tolerance is explicit. Individual records, query results, and computed aggregates each have different invalidation needs.

Design considerations

Include every result-changing input in the key, including tenant and authorization scope where relevant. Limit value size and avoid caching arbitrary one-off queries indefinitely. Negative caching can reduce repeated misses, but its expiration must allow newly created data to appear.

cards.title: Cache-aside
cards.question: Explain cache-aside and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

With cache-aside, the application checks the cache first. On a miss it loads the authoritative value, stores a cache entry, and returns the result. The application also manages invalidation around writes.

Design considerations

Concurrent misses can repeat expensive work; use request coalescing or a suitable lock. A read racing with invalidation can repopulate stale data. TTLs, versioned values, and carefully ordered writes help bound or prevent that behavior, depending on the consistency requirement.

cards.title: Write-through
cards.question: Explain write-through and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Write-through makes updating the cache part of the write path to durable storage. This can improve cache readiness for later reads, but the extra work adds latency and couples write availability to another component.

Design considerations

Define which system is authoritative and what happens if only one update succeeds. A cache should not acknowledge durability that the backing store has not provided. Use a protocol with clear failure handling; two ordinary writes do not automatically form an atomic transaction.

cards.title: Write-behind (write-back)
cards.question: Explain write-behind (write-back) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Write-behind acknowledges a write before asynchronously propagating it to the backing store. Batching can improve throughput, but the buffered updates become part of the durability and correctness design.

Design considerations

Specify whether the buffer is durable, how writes are ordered, and how retries are deduplicated. Bound backlog size and apply backpressure. Crashes, eviction, and shutdown must not silently discard acknowledged changes. This tradeoff is inappropriate when those guarantees cannot be met.

cards.title: Refresh-ahead
cards.question: Explain refresh-ahead and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Refresh-ahead starts reloading an entry before it expires, aiming to keep frequently used data ready. It can reduce latency spikes caused by popular entries expiring at the same time.

Design considerations

Base refresh decisions on actual demand and stagger schedules with jitter. A failed refresh may leave a usable stale value only if the application permits it. Avoid refreshing cold keys forever, and prevent many workers from refreshing the same key simultaneously.

cards.title: Asynchronism
cards.question: Explain asynchronism and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Asynchronous work separates accepting a request from completing all of its effects. A queue or durable log can buffer bursts and let workers process tasks independently. The user-visible contract must explain when results become available.

Design considerations

Assume tasks may be retried unless the system proves otherwise. Use idempotent handlers, retry limits, backoff, dead-letter handling, and observable job status. Queue depth and age reveal overload; an ever-growing queue is not a solution to insufficient capacity.

cards.title: Communication
cards.question: Explain communication and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Services communicate through request/response calls, events, streams, and queued jobs. The choice affects coupling, latency, ordering, and failure handling. A successful network send does not necessarily mean the business operation completed.

Design considerations

Specify deadlines, payload limits, authentication, versioning, and retry semantics. Distinguish transport errors from application errors. For multi-step workflows, define how to detect partial completion and compensate or resume without repeating irreversible effects.

cards.title: Hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP)
cards.question: Explain hypertext transfer protocol (http) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

HTTP defines request methods, response status codes, headers, and representation semantics. Different protocol versions transport those semantics differently: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC.

Design considerations

Use method semantics deliberately, including safe reads and idempotent operations. Cache behavior depends on explicit response policies and validation. Budget connection and response time, use HTTPS, and define application-level idempotency for retried operations that create side effects.

cards.title: Transmission control protocol (TCP)
cards.question: Explain transmission control protocol (tcp) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints. It handles retransmission and congestion control, but does not preserve application message boundaries or guarantee that a remote application committed a request.

Design considerations

Define framing and deadlines above the stream. A stalled byte sequence can delay later bytes, and a disconnected client may not know whether a write took effect. Connection reuse helps avoid setup overhead, while application retries still need correctness rules.

cards.title: User datagram protocol (UDP)
cards.question: Explain user datagram protocol (udp) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

UDP sends datagrams without providing built-in delivery confirmation, ordering, or duplicate suppression. Applications that need those properties must supply them themselves or use a protocol layered above UDP.

Design considerations

Consider packet loss, reordering, size limits, congestion behavior, and NAT traversal. UDP is useful when the application controls latency and reliability tradeoffs. Its small transport header does not make every UDP-based application faster or simpler than a TCP-based alternative.

cards.title: Remote procedure call (RPC)
cards.question: Explain remote procedure call (rpc) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

RPC presents a remote operation as an interface with typed or structured inputs and outputs. Tooling may generate clients and handle serialization, but the remote call remains subject to latency, timeouts, and partial failure.

Design considerations

Design interfaces with deadlines, cancellation, compatibility, and idempotency in mind. Avoid chatty calls that multiply network trips. Document retryable errors and partial results. A local-looking method signature should not hide the operational consequences of a network boundary.

cards.title: Representational state transfer (REST)
cards.question: Explain representational state transfer (rest) and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

REST is an architectural style centered on resources, representations, a uniform interface, and stateless interactions. An HTTP API can use resource-oriented URLs and method semantics, but JSON over HTTP alone does not establish every REST constraint.

Design considerations

Use stable resource identifiers, explicit status codes, pagination, validation, and caching where appropriate. Keep authentication separate from resource naming. Model long-running work as a resource with observable state rather than holding every request open indefinitely.

cards.title: Security
cards.question: Explain security and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Start from the assets being protected and the actors allowed to access them. Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform a particular operation on a particular resource. Both are required.

Design considerations

Apply least privilege, input validation, output encoding, transport encryption, and secure secret storage. Check authorization on each relevant operation, including object-level access. Add rate limits, audit trails, dependency updates, and recovery procedures; no single component replaces a threat model.

cards.title: Powers of two table
cards.question: Explain powers of two table and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Binary capacity calculations use powers of two. A kibibyte (KiB) is 2^10 bytes, a mebibyte (MiB) is 2^20, and a gibibyte (GiB) is 2^30. Decimal KB, MB, and GB use powers of ten.

Design considerations

Make units explicit in estimates. For example, 8 GiB divided into 4 KiB pages gives 2^21 pages before accounting for metadata. Reserve capacity for indexes, replication, buffers, and growth rather than treating all installed memory as usable payload storage.

cards.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know
cards.question: Explain latency numbers every programmer should know and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Latency estimates help identify which operations dominate a request, but fixed historical tables are not universal hardware specifications. Memory access, storage, network distance, contention, and payload size all affect the result.

Design considerations

Build a budget from measurements in the target environment. Compare in-process work, local storage, intra-region calls, and cross-region calls as separate tiers. Include serialization, queueing, and tail behavior. Parallel independent calls can reduce elapsed time, while sequential calls add their delays.

cards.title: MD5
cards.question: Explain md5 and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

MD5 produces a 128-bit digest. It is unsuitable for security designs that require collision resistance, and fast unsalted hashes are unsuitable for storing passwords. A hash function’s output length alone does not establish its security.

Design considerations

Use a currently appropriate cryptographic construction for the specific purpose, including authenticated integrity or password hashing. For non-adversarial checksums, state the failure model explicitly. Hashes do not eliminate collisions, so identifier designs still need a collision policy.

cards.title: Base 62
cards.question: Explain base 62 and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Base 62 encodes numbers using an alphabet of 62 symbols, commonly digits plus uppercase and lowercase letters. With a fixed alphabet order, conversion repeatedly divides by 62 and records remainders.

Design considerations

Specify the alphabet, zero representation, case sensitivity, and leading-zero policy. Encoding is reversible and does not provide secrecy. A short-link service also needs unique identifier allocation, collision handling for random IDs, and protections against enumeration when appropriate.

cards.title: What is HATEOAS?
cards.question: Describe HATEOAS and the tradeoffs you would discuss in an API design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

Hypermedia as the engine of application state means that responses include links or controls describing available next actions. A client follows those controls using understood relationship names, rather than constructing every future URL from a separate fixed map.

Design considerations

For example, an order representation might expose a cancellation action only while cancellation is allowed. Hypermedia can help evolve navigation, but clients still need to understand the domain and representation format. Balance the extra structure with the needs of actual consumers.

cards.title: RPC and REST calls comparison
cards.question: Explain rpc and rest calls comparison and the tradeoffs you would discuss in a system design interview.
cards.answer:
Explanation

RPC emphasizes operations such as approving an order; resource-oriented HTTP APIs emphasize resources and their representations. Both can use HTTP, and both still need authorization, versioning, deadlines, and clearly specified error behavior.

Design considerations

An operation-style interface might expose approveOrder(id). A resource-oriented alternative could create an approval record under an order. Choose the model that makes invariants and workflows clear; changing a URL or HTTP verb does not by itself change a system’s reliability or coupling.

cards.title: Design Mint.com
cards.question: Design Mint.com
cards.answer:
Note: This document links directly to relevant areas found in the system design topics to avoid duplication. Refer to the linked content for general talking points, tradeoffs, and alternatives.

Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

Without an interviewer to address clarifying questions, we'll define some use cases and constraints.

Use cases

We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

  • User connects to a financial account
  • Service extracts transactions from the account
    • Updates daily
    • Categorizes transactions
      • Allows manual category override by the user
      • No automatic re-categorization
    • Analyzes monthly spending, by category
  • Service recommends a budget
    • Allows users to manually set a budget
    • Sends notifications when approaching or exceeding budget
  • Service has high availability

Out of scope

  • Service performs additional logging and analytics

Constraints and assumptions

State assumptions

  • Traffic is not evenly distributed
  • Automatic daily update of accounts applies only to users active in the past 30 days
  • Adding or removing financial accounts is relatively rare
  • Budget notifications don't need to be instant
  • 10 million users
    • 10 budget categories per user = 100 million budget items
    • Example categories:
      • Housing = $1,000
      • Food = $200
      • Gas = $100
    • Sellers are used to determine transaction category
      • 50,000 sellers
  • 30 million financial accounts
  • 5 billion transactions per month
  • 500 million read requests per month
  • 10:1 write to read ratio
    • Write-heavy, users make transactions daily, but few visit the site daily

Calculate usage

Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.

  • Size per transaction:
    • user_id - 8 bytes
    • created_at - 5 bytes
    • seller - 32 bytes
    • amount - 5 bytes
    • Total: ~50 bytes
  • 250 GB of new transaction content per month
    • 50 bytes per transaction * 5 billion transactions per month
    • 9 TB of new transaction content in 3 years
    • Assume most are new transactions instead of updates to existing ones
  • 2,000 transactions per second on average
  • 200 read requests per second on average

Handy conversion guide:

  • 2.5 million seconds per month
  • 1 request per second = 2.5 million requests per month
  • 40 requests per second = 100 million requests per month
  • 400 requests per second = 1 billion requests per month

Step 2: Create a high level design

Outline a high level design with all important components.

Step 3: Design core components

Dive into details for each core component.

Use case: User connects to a financial account

We could store info on the 10 million users in a relational database. We should discuss the use cases and tradeoffs between choosing SQL or NoSQL.

  • The Client sends a request to the Web Server, running as a reverse proxy
  • The Web Server forwards the request to the Accounts API server
  • The Accounts API server updates the SQL Database accounts table with the newly entered account info

Clarify with your interviewer how much code you are expected to write.

The accounts table could have the following structure:

id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT
created_at datetime NOT NULL
last_update datetime NOT NULL
account_url varchar(255) NOT NULL
account_login varchar(32) NOT NULL
account_password_hash char(64) NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id, user_id, and created_at to speed up lookups (log-time instead of scanning the entire table) and to keep the data in memory. Reading 1 MB sequentially from memory takes about 250 microseconds, while reading from SSD takes 4x and from disk takes 80x longer.1

We'll use a public REST API:

$ curl -X POST --data '{ "user_id": "foo", "account_url": "bar", \
    "account_login": "baz", "account_password": "qux" }' \
    https://mint.com/api/v1/account

For internal communications, we could use Remote Procedure Calls.

Next, the service extracts transactions from the account.

Use case: Service extracts transactions from the account

We'll want to extract information from an account in these cases:

  • The user first links the account
  • The user manually refreshes the account
  • Automatically each day for users who have been active in the past 30 days

Data flow:

  • The Client sends a request to the Web Server
  • The Web Server forwards the request to the Accounts API server
  • The Accounts API server places a job on a Queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ
    • Extracting transactions could take awhile, we'd probably want to do this asynchronously with a queue, although this introduces additional complexity
  • The Transaction Extraction Service does the following:
    • Pulls from the Queue and extracts transactions for the given account from the financial institution, storing the results as raw log files in the Object Store
    • Uses the Category Service to categorize each transaction
    • Uses the Budget Service to calculate aggregate monthly spending by category
      • The Budget Service uses the Notification Service to let users know if they are nearing or have exceeded their budget
    • Updates the SQL Database transactions table with categorized transactions
    • Updates the SQL Database monthly_spending table with aggregate monthly spending by category
    • Notifies the user the transactions have completed through the Notification Service:
      • Uses a Queue (not pictured) to asynchronously send out notifications

The transactions table could have the following structure:

id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT
created_at datetime NOT NULL
seller varchar(32) NOT NULL
amount decimal NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id, user_id, and created_at.

The monthly_spending table could have the following structure:

id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT
month_year date NOT NULL
category varchar(32)
amount decimal NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id and user_id.

Category service

For the Category Service, we can seed a seller-to-category dictionary with the most popular sellers. If we estimate 50,000 sellers and estimate each entry to take less than 255 bytes, the dictionary would only take about 12 MB of memory.

Clarify with your interviewer how much code you are expected to write.

class DefaultCategories(Enum):

    HOUSING = 0
    FOOD = 1
    GAS = 2
    SHOPPING = 3
    ...

seller_category_map = {}
seller_category_map['Exxon'] = DefaultCategories.GAS
seller_category_map['Target'] = DefaultCategories.SHOPPING
...

For sellers not initially seeded in the map, we could use a crowdsourcing effort by evaluating the manual category overrides our users provide. We could use a heap to quickly lookup the top manual override per seller in O(1) time.

class Categorizer(object):

    def __init__(self, seller_category_map, self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map):
        self.seller_category_map = seller_category_map
        self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map = \
            seller_category_crowd_overrides_map

    def categorize(self, transaction):
        if transaction.seller in self.seller_category_map:
            return self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller]
        elif transaction.seller in self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map:
            self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller] = \
                self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map[transaction.seller].peek_min()
            return self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller]
        return None

Transaction implementation:

class Transaction(object):

    def __init__(self, created_at, seller, amount):
        self.timestamp = timestamp
        self.seller = seller
        self.amount = amount

Use case: Service recommends a budget

To start, we could use a generic budget template that allocates category amounts based on income tiers. Using this approach, we would not have to store the 100 million budget items identified in the constraints, only those that the user overrides. If a user overrides a budget category, which we could store the override in the TABLE budget_overrides.

class Budget(object):

    def __init__(self, income):
        self.income = income
        self.categories_to_budget_map = self.create_budget_template()

    def create_budget_template(self):
        return {
            'DefaultCategories.HOUSING': income * .4,
            'DefaultCategories.FOOD': income * .2
            'DefaultCategories.GAS': income * .1,
            'DefaultCategories.SHOPPING': income * .2
            ...
        }

    def override_category_budget(self, category, amount):
        self.categories_to_budget_map[category] = amount

For the Budget Service, we can potentially run SQL queries on the transactions table to generate the monthly_spending aggregate table. The monthly_spending table would likely have much fewer rows than the total 5 billion transactions, since users typically have many transactions per month.

As an alternative, we can run MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files to:

  • Categorize each transaction
  • Generate aggregate monthly spending by category

Running analyses on the transaction files could significantly reduce the load on the database.

We could call the Budget Service to re-run the analysis if the user updates a category.

Clarify with your interviewer how much code you are expected to write.

Sample log file format, tab delimited:

user_id   timestamp   seller  amount

MapReduce implementation:

class SpendingByCategory(MRJob):

    def __init__(self, categorizer):
        self.categorizer = categorizer
        self.current_year_month = calc_current_year_month()
        ...

    def calc_current_year_month(self):
        """Return the current year and month."""
        ...

    def extract_year_month(self, timestamp):
        """Return the year and month portions of the timestamp."""
        ...

    def handle_budget_notifications(self, key, total):
        """Call notification API if nearing or exceeded budget."""
        ...

    def mapper(self, _, line):
        """Parse each log line, extract and transform relevant lines.

        Argument line will be of the form:

        user_id   timestamp   seller  amount

        Using the categorizer to convert seller to category,
        emit key value pairs of the form:

        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 25
        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 100
        (user_id, 2016-01, gas), 50
        """
        user_id, timestamp, seller, amount = line.split('\t')
        category = self.categorizer.categorize(seller)
        period = self.extract_year_month(timestamp)
        if period == self.current_year_month:
            yield (user_id, period, category), amount

    def reducer(self, key, value):
        """Sum values for each key.

        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 125
        (user_id, 2016-01, gas), 50
        """
        total = sum(values)
        yield key, sum(values)

Step 4: Scale the design

Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

Important: Do not simply jump right into the final design from the initial design!

State you would 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating alternatives and trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS as a sample on how to iteratively scale the initial design.

It's important to discuss what bottlenecks you might encounter with the initial design and how you might address each of them. For example, what issues are addressed by adding a Load Balancer with multiple Web Servers? CDN?Master-Slave Replicas? What are the alternatives and Trade-Offs for each?

We'll introduce some components to complete the design and to address scalability issues. Internal load balancers are not shown to reduce clutter.

To avoid repeating discussions, refer to the following system design topics for main talking points, tradeoffs, and alternatives:

  • DNS
  • CDN
  • Load balancer
  • Horizontal scaling
  • Web server (reverse proxy)
  • API server (application layer)
  • Cache
  • Relational database management system (RDBMS)
  • SQL write master-slave failover
  • Master-slave replication
  • Asynchronism
  • Consistency patterns
  • Availability patterns

We'll add an additional use case: User accesses summaries and transactions.

User sessions, aggregate stats by category, and recent transactions could be placed in a Memory Cache such as Redis or Memcached.

  • The Client sends a read request to the Web Server
  • The Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server
    • Static content can be served from the Object Store such as S3, which is cached on the CDN
  • The Read API server does the following:
    • Checks the Memory Cache for the content
      • If the url is in the Memory Cache, returns the cached contents
      • Else
        • If the url is in the SQL Database, fetches the contents
          • Updates the Memory Cache with the contents

Refer to When to update the cache for tradeoffs and alternatives. The approach above describes cache-aside.

Instead of keeping the monthly_spending aggregate table in the SQL Database, we could create a separate Analytics Database using a data warehousing solution such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery.

We might only want to store a month of transactions data in the database, while storing the rest in a data warehouse or in an Object Store. An Object Store such as Amazon S3 can comfortably handle the constraint of 250 GB of new content per month.

To address the 2,000 average read requests per second (higher at peak), traffic for popular content should be handled by the Memory Cache instead of the database. The Memory Cache is also useful for handling the unevenly distributed traffic and traffic spikes. The SQL Read Replicas should be able to handle the cache misses, as long as the replicas are not bogged down with replicating writes.

200 average transaction writes per second (higher at peak) might be tough for a single SQL Write Master-Slave. We might need to employ additional SQL scaling patterns:

  • Federation
  • Sharding
  • Denormalization
  • SQL Tuning

We should also consider moving some data to a NoSQL Database.

Additional talking points

Additional topics to dive into, depending on the problem scope and time remaining.

NoSQL

  • Key-value store
  • Document store
  • Wide column store
  • Graph database
  • SQL vs NoSQL

Caching

  • Where to cache
    • Client caching
    • CDN caching
    • Web server caching
    • Database caching
    • Application caching
  • What to cache
    • Caching at the database query level
    • Caching at the object level
  • When to update the cache
    • Cache-aside
    • Write-through
    • Write-behind (write-back)
    • Refresh ahead

Asynchronism and microservices

  • Message queues
  • Task queues
  • Back pressure
  • Microservices

Communications

  • Discuss tradeoffs:
    • External communication with clients - HTTP APIs following REST
    • Internal communications - RPC
  • Service discovery

Security

Refer to the security section.

Latency numbers

See Latency numbers every programmer should know.

Ongoing

  • Continue benchmarking and monitoring your system to address bottlenecks as they come up
  • Scaling is an iterative process

last_update datetime NOT NULL
account_url varchar(255) NOT NULL
account_login varchar(32) NOT NULL
account_password_hash char(64) NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id, user_id, and created_at to speed up lookups (log-time instead of scanning the entire table) and to keep the data in memory. Reading 1 MB sequentially from memory takes about 250 microseconds, while reading from SSD takes 4x and from disk takes 80x longer.1

We'll use a public REST API:

$ curl -X POST --data '{ "user_id": "foo", "account_url": "bar", \
    "account_login": "baz", "account_password": "qux" }' \
    https://mint.com/api/v1/account

For internal communications, we could use Remote Procedure Calls.

Next, the service extracts transactions from the account.

sections.title: Use case: Service extracts transactions from the account
sections.html:
We'll want to extract information from an account in these cases:

  • The user first links the account
  • The user manually refreshes the account
  • Automatically each day for users who have been active in the past 30 days

Data flow:

  • The Client sends a request to the Web Server
  • The Web Server forwards the request to the Accounts API server
  • The Accounts API server places a job on a Queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ
    • Extracting transactions could take awhile, we'd probably want to do this asynchronously with a queue, although this introduces additional complexity
  • The Transaction Extraction Service does the following:
    • Pulls from the Queue and extracts transactions for the given account from the financial institution, storing the results as raw log files in the Object Store
    • Uses the Category Service to categorize each transaction
    • Uses the Budget Service to calculate aggregate monthly spending by category
      • The Budget Service uses the Notification Service to let users know if they are nearing or have exceeded their budget
    • Updates the SQL Database transactions table with categorized transactions
    • Updates the SQL Database monthly_spending table with aggregate monthly spending by category
    • Notifies the user the transactions have completed through the Notification Service:
      • Uses a Queue (not pictured) to asynchronously send out notifications

The transactions table could have the following structure:

id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT
created_at datetime NOT NULL
seller varchar(32) NOT NULL
amount decimal NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id, user_id, and created_at.

The monthly_spending table could have the following structure:

id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT
month_year date NOT NULL
category varchar(32)
amount decimal NOT NULL
user_id int NOT NULL
PRIMARY KEY(id)
FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)

We'll create an index on id and user_id.

sections.title: Category service
sections.html:
For the Category Service, we can seed a seller-to-category dictionary with the most popular sellers. If we estimate 50,000 sellers and estimate each entry to take less than 255 bytes, the dictionary would only take about 12 MB of memory.

Clarify with your interviewer how much code you are expected to write.

class DefaultCategories(Enum):

    HOUSING = 0
    FOOD = 1
    GAS = 2
    SHOPPING = 3
    ...

seller_category_map = {}
seller_category_map['Exxon'] = DefaultCategories.GAS
seller_category_map['Target'] = DefaultCategories.SHOPPING
...

For sellers not initially seeded in the map, we could use a crowdsourcing effort by evaluating the manual category overrides our users provide. We could use a heap to quickly lookup the top manual override per seller in O(1) time.

class Categorizer(object):

    def __init__(self, seller_category_map, self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map):
        self.seller_category_map = seller_category_map
        self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map = \
            seller_category_crowd_overrides_map

    def categorize(self, transaction):
        if transaction.seller in self.seller_category_map:
            return self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller]
        elif transaction.seller in self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map:
            self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller] = \
                self.seller_category_crowd_overrides_map[transaction.seller].peek_min()
            return self.seller_category_map[transaction.seller]
        return None

Transaction implementation:

class Transaction(object):

    def __init__(self, created_at, seller, amount):
        self.timestamp = timestamp
        self.seller = seller
        self.amount = amount

sections.title: Use case: Service recommends a budget
sections.html:
To start, we could use a generic budget template that allocates category amounts based on income tiers. Using this approach, we would not have to store the 100 million budget items identified in the constraints, only those that the user overrides. If a user overrides a budget category, which we could store the override in the TABLE budget_overrides.

class Budget(object):

    def __init__(self, income):
        self.income = income
        self.categories_to_budget_map = self.create_budget_template()

    def create_budget_template(self):
        return {
            'DefaultCategories.HOUSING': income * .4,
            'DefaultCategories.FOOD': income * .2
            'DefaultCategories.GAS': income * .1,
            'DefaultCategories.SHOPPING': income * .2
            ...
        }

    def override_category_budget(self, category, amount):
        self.categories_to_budget_map[category] = amount

For the Budget Service, we can potentially run SQL queries on the transactions table to generate the monthly_spending aggregate table. The monthly_spending table would likely have much fewer rows than the total 5 billion transactions, since users typically have many transactions per month.

As an alternative, we can run MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files to:

  • Categorize each transaction
  • Generate aggregate monthly spending by category

Running analyses on the transaction files could significantly reduce the load on the database.

We could call the Budget Service to re-run the analysis if the user updates a category.

Clarify with your interviewer how much code you are expected to write.

Sample log file format, tab delimited:

user_id   timestamp   seller  amount

MapReduce implementation:

class SpendingByCategory(MRJob):

    def __init__(self, categorizer):
        self.categorizer = categorizer
        self.current_year_month = calc_current_year_month()
        ...

    def calc_current_year_month(self):
        """Return the current year and month."""
        ...

    def extract_year_month(self, timestamp):
        """Return the year and month portions of the timestamp."""
        ...

    def handle_budget_notifications(self, key, total):
        """Call notification API if nearing or exceeded budget."""
        ...

    def mapper(self, _, line):
        """Parse each log line, extract and transform relevant lines.

        Argument line will be of the form:

        user_id   timestamp   seller  amount

        Using the categorizer to convert seller to category,
        emit key value pairs of the form:

        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 25
        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 100
        (user_id, 2016-01, gas), 50
        """
        user_id, timestamp, seller, amount = line.split('\t')
        category = self.categorizer.categorize(seller)
        period = self.extract_year_month(timestamp)
        if period == self.current_year_month:
            yield (user_id, period, category), amount

    def reducer(self, key, value):
        """Sum values for each key.

        (user_id, 2016-01, shopping), 125
        (user_id, 2016-01, gas), 50
        """
        total = sum(values)
        yield key, sum(values)

sections.title: Step 4: Scale the design
sections.html:
Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

Important: Do not simply jump right into the final design from the initial design!

State you would 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating alternatives and trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS as a sample on how to iteratively scale the initial design.

It's important to discuss what bottlenecks you might encounter with the initial design and how you might address each of them. For example, what issues are addressed by adding a Load Balancer with multiple Web Servers? CDN?Master-Slave Replicas? What are the alternatives and Trade-Offs for each?

We'll introduce some components to complete the design and to address scalability issues. Internal load balancers are not shown to reduce clutter.

To avoid repeating discussions, refer to the following system design topics for main talking points, tradeoffs, and alternatives:

  • DNS
  • CDN
  • Load balancer
  • Horizontal scaling
  • Web server (reverse proxy)
  • API server (application layer)
  • Cache
  • Relational database management system (RDBMS)
  • SQL write master-slave failover
  • Master-slave replication
  • Asynchronism
  • Consistency patterns
  • Availability patterns

We'll add an additional use case: User accesses summaries and transactions.

User sessions, aggregate stats by category, and recent transactions could be placed in a Memory Cache such as Redis or Memcached.

  • The Client sends a read request to the Web Server
  • The Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server
    • Static content can be served from the Object Store such as S3, which is cached on the CDN
  • The Read API server does the following:
    • Checks the Memory Cache for the content
      • If the url is in the Memory Cache, returns the cached contents
      • Else
        • If the url is in the SQL Database, fetches the contents
          • Updates the Memory Cache with the contents

Refer to When to update the cache for tradeoffs and alternatives. The approach above describes cache-aside.

Instead of keeping the monthly_spending aggregate table in the SQL Database, we could create a separate Analytics Database using a data warehousing solution such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery.

We might only want to store a month of transactions data in the database, while storing the rest in a data warehouse or in an Object Store. An Object Store such as Amazon S3 can comfortably handle the constraint of 250 GB of new content per month.

To address the 2,000 average read requests per second (higher at peak), traffic for popular content should be handled by the Memory Cache instead of the database. The Memory Cache is also useful for handling the unevenly distributed traffic and traffic spikes. The SQL Read Replicas should be able to handle the cache misses, as long as the replicas are not bogged down with replicating writes.

200 average transaction writes per second (higher at peak) might be tough for a single SQL Write Master-Slave. We might need to employ additional SQL scaling patterns:

  • Federation
  • Sharding
  • Denormalization
  • SQL Tuning

We should also consider moving some data to a NoSQL Database.

  • Microservices

sections.title: Communications
sections.html:
