cards.title: Isolate mutable retry request snapshots
cards.question:
A retry test builds attempts with Array(count).fill(request) in JavaScript or [request] * count in Python. Mutating attempt 0's nested headers unexpectedly changes other attempts. Implement buildAttempts(request,count) so the original and every attempt have independent nested data.

Contract

  • The request is a finite JSON-like tree of objects/dictionaries, arrays/lists, strings, booleans, null/None, and numbers. It contains no functions, custom classes, cycles, or shared-reference identity requirements.
  • count is a nonnegative integer. Each attempt must be a full deep snapshot taken before the function returns.

Examples to reason through

  • After creating two attempts, change attempts[0].headers.tags[0]; attempts[1] and the original must keep their prior tag.
  • count=0 → []; empty request still yields independent objects.
cards.answer:
Both array fill and list multiplication duplicate references, not nested objects. A shallow spread/dict copy only separates the outer container. Deep-copy separately for each attempt: structuredClone in JavaScript and copy.deepcopy in Python support this contract. A deep copy is independent but remains mutable; immutability is a separate policy.

Complexity: O(count × size(request)) time and output space, plus traversal memory for cloning one request.

cards.title: Design an offline-first review app
cards.question:
Design a study app that remains useful on a phone during a week without connectivity, then reconciles progress across two devices. Explain storage, synchronization, conflict behavior, and updates.

Requirements

  • Reading downloaded decks and recording reviews must work offline after initial installation/download.
  • A review must not disappear or be counted twice after reconnecting. Note edits from two devices must not silently overwrite each other.
  • Users need a visible download state, pending-sync count, and portable export.

Assumed scale

Assume 50,000 daily active users × 200 reviews/day = 10 million review events/day, about 116/s average and 1,200/s at a 10× peak. At 256 bytes/event, raw events are about 2.56 GB/day before indexes and replication. A typical device caches 20 MB of deck data.
cards.answer:
Separate immutable deck assets, local user state, and a durable outbox of pending operations. The app renders from local state immediately and synchronizes in the background when it can.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Draw two separate flows: the local transaction and the later server acknowledgement. Identify which side owns each identifier and cursor.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Separate immutable deck assets, local user state, and a durable outbox of pending operations. The app renders from local state immediately and synchronizes in the background when it can.
  • Use a service worker to cache a versioned application shell/deck assets and IndexedDB for structured progress plus the outbox. Commit the local review and its outbox event in one transaction. Display a ready-for-offline status only after required assets are cached.
  • Give each operation a device-generated unique ID and tenant/user scope. POST batches with these IDs; the server deduplicates transactionally, assigns a monotone server sequence, and returns acknowledgements plus a pull cursor. Delete acknowledged outbox entries only after their acknowledgements are durable locally.
  • Model reviews as append-only events so concurrent devices can both contribute. State a deterministic scheduling policy: for example, process accepted review events in server sequence order and recompute the card schedule. Device timestamps remain display metadata because clocks can disagree. Deduplication removes retries, not genuinely separate reviews.
  • For notes, send the base revision. If it is stale, retain both versions and offer a merge instead of last-write-wins data loss. Keep deck content version separate from progress IDs so a content update does not reset learning history.
  • Coordinate shell/deck/schema upgrades, provide a recoverable export, and test storage eviction. A browser can remove local data; offline storage alone is not a backup. Reauthenticate on reconnect, scope caches by account, and clear private local data on an explicit sign-out policy.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• An append-only review log simplifies retry handling and auditability but needs compaction/checkpoints for long histories.
  • Automatic conflict resolution feels smooth but needs a product rule; preserving both note edits is safer when intent cannot be inferred.
  • Download-on-demand reduces storage; downloading all chosen decks gives a stronger offline promise. Background execution differs by mobile platform, so sync-on-open must work.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Kill the app between local write and upload, and between server commit and response; repeated uploads must converge without missing reviews.
  • Edit the same note on two offline devices, skew a device clock, update the deck while offline, and exhaust storage.
  • Install online, confirm caching, disable all network, reopen from the home screen, review cards, then reconnect and verify counts.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you support encrypted private notes, account switching, tombstones for deletions, or a device returning after a year?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Defines offline readiness and transaction boundaries.
  • Shows duplicate suppression and a concrete conflict policy.
  • Distinguishes cache availability from durable backup and explains update recovery.

cards.title: Make a job-creation API safe to retry
cards.question:
Design POST /render-jobs so a client can safely retry after a timeout without creating a second rendering job. Cover two identical requests arriving concurrently and the server crashing after commit but before replying.

Requirements

  • Clients supply a stable idempotency key for one intended creation.
  • The same key and same request return the original job; reusing a key for a different request is rejected.
  • The guarantee lasts 24 hours and is scoped to the authenticated tenant. Job execution is asynchronous.

Assumed scale

Assume 100 new jobs/s and a 24-hour deduplication window: 8.64 million active idempotency records. At an illustrative 200 bytes/record, raw records alone use about 1.73 GB; account separately for indexes, request hashes, and response data.
cards.answer:
Make (tenant_id, idempotency_key) a unique database key. Store a canonical request digest, job ID, creation status, and expiry. Authenticate and authorize before lookup; the key is not an authorization token.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Choose a single transaction that joins the intent record, resource creation, and reliable enqueueing.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Make (tenant_id, idempotency_key) a unique database key. Store a canonical request digest, job ID, creation status, and expiry. Authenticate and authorize before lookup; the key is not an authorization token.
  • In one database transaction, reserve the idempotency key, create the job row, and write an outbox row for execution. A concurrent duplicate is serialized by the uniqueness constraint; after the winning transaction completes, compare its request digest and return its job ID or a mismatch error.
  • If the transaction aborts, none of those rows should remain committed. If commit succeeds but the response is lost, a retry reads the committed record and returns the same outcome. Do not claim that a pre-check followed by a separate insert is race-free.
  • An outbox relay publishes pending jobs and records its progress. Publishing may happen twice if it crashes between publish and marking sent, so workers use the job ID to make state transitions idempotent. External side effects require their own deduplication protocol.
  • Document key retention and expiry precisely. A request replayed after the window may create a new job; clients needing longer protection must retain a business operation ID or use a longer policy. Bound key length and per-tenant storage abuse.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Persisting the original response provides exact replay but uses more storage than retaining a canonical resource ID.
  • Hashing the request alone is not an intent identifier: two identical jobs may be intentionally separate. A caller-chosen key represents intent.
  • A distributed cache can speed lookup, but correctness should live in an atomic durable boundary, with careful expiry semantics.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Fire 100 simultaneous same-key requests; assert one job row and one logical execution.
  • Drop the response after commit, fail the outbox relay after publication, and replay a request after expiry.
  • Reuse a key with a changed payload and from a different tenant; verify mismatch handling and tenant isolation.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you support operations that take minutes, retryable versus terminal failures, and a non-idempotent external rendering provider?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Specifies the key's scope, retention, and payload-mismatch behavior.
  • Handles concurrent duplicates and the commit/response failure window.
  • Separates request deduplication from end-to-end execution guarantees.

cards.title: Protect a multi-tenant API from bursts
cards.question:
Design per-tenant admission control for a shared API. A tenant should sustain 100 requests/s and briefly burst to 200 requests without overwhelming shared backends.

Requirements

  • Return a clear rejection response and useful retry guidance when the tenant budget is exhausted.
  • Protect the backend with a global concurrency/load limit as well as per-tenant fairness.
  • Explain behavior during limiter failure and across two regions.

Assumed scale

Assume 1,000 active tenants and 20,000 incoming requests/s total, with heavily skewed traffic. A typical admitted request holds backend resources for 100 ms; 20,000 requests/s at that mean duration implies roughly 2,000 concurrent requests before queues and overhead.
cards.answer:
Use one token bucket per tenant: capacity 200, refill 100 tokens/s. On arrival, refill by elapsed time up to capacity, then atomically consume one token if available. Store balance and last-refill time together at the limiter's authoritative shard.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Write the bucket state and atomic update first. Then identify the guarantee lost when you add replicas or fallbacks.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Use one token bucket per tenant: capacity 200, refill 100 tokens/s. On arrival, refill by elapsed time up to capacity, then atomically consume one token if available. Store balance and last-refill time together at the limiter's authoritative shard.
  • Use a single atomic operation or server-side script for read/refill/decrement; separate reads and writes overspend under concurrency. Base elapsed time on a consistent server clock and clamp negative elapsed time. Expire inactive buckets only after enough time to refill fully.
  • A depleted bucket returns HTTP 429 with a retry delay derived from the deficit. Clients apply bounded backoff with jitter. Rate limiting does not replace a concurrency cap, bounded queue, deadlines, or shedding low-priority work under backend overload.
  • Choose failure behavior by endpoint: strict fail-closed for costly scarce operations; a small local emergency allowance for a read endpoint that can tolerate bounded overshoot. Record fallback activations and make the overshoot bound explicit.
  • For two regions, either route a tenant to one authoritative bucket, coordinate globally at added latency, or allocate regional quotas whose sum stays within the global budget. Independently issuing the full quota in both regions doubles the allowed rate. Rebalancing quota requires careful ownership and failure handling.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Central coordination strengthens the global limit but adds latency and a dependency; local buckets are faster but can overshoot.
  • Token buckets permit controlled bursts; sliding logs track exact recent arrivals but cost more memory and work.
  • A tenant's rate is only one dimension: request cost, active streams, or tokens may be more meaningful than raw request count.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Send simultaneous requests at refill boundaries, idle then burst, skew clocks, and fail the authoritative shard.
  • Create one hot tenant, rebalance regions, and prove the maximum overshoot under fallback.
  • Measure admitted/rejected requests by bounded labels, limiter latency, backend saturation, and queue age.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Support weighted requests, tenant priorities, long-lived streaming calls, or a limit that must never be exceeded globally.

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Derives refill and burst behavior and includes atomicity.
  • Distinguishes rate, concurrency, queue length, and overload.
  • Quantifies the consistency/failure trade-off instead of assuming global correctness from local counters.

cards.title: Deliver webhooks despite retries and outages
cards.question:
Design a webhook delivery service that accepts tenant events, reliably attempts delivery to registered destinations, and tolerates duplicates, slow receivers, and multi-hour outages.

Requirements

  • Persist events before acknowledging acceptance. Retry transient failures with bounded backoff; preserve terminal failures for inspection/replay.
  • Give each event a stable delivery identity and authenticate payloads.
  • Do not claim exactly-once business side effects at an arbitrary receiver.

Assumed scale

Assume 500 events/s × 1 KB/event = about 43.2 GB/day of raw payloads. A six-hour destination outage can accumulate 10.8 million events if all traffic targets it; isolate that backlog so healthy tenants continue.
cards.answer:
Accept the event into durable storage and enqueue an event reference through a transaction/outbox boundary. Partition work by tenant or destination and enforce per-destination concurrency so one slow endpoint cannot occupy the entire worker fleet.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Walk through the ambiguous outcome after a receiver commits but the sender times out. No broker setting can remove that ambiguity by itself.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Accept the event into durable storage and enqueue an event reference through a transaction/outbox boundary. Partition work by tenant or destination and enforce per-destination concurrency so one slow endpoint cannot occupy the entire worker fleet.
  • A worker acquires a bounded lease, signs the payload with a rotating destination secret, and sends a stable event ID plus a timestamp. Apply connection and total deadlines, response-size limits, and a configured egress policy for registered URLs.
  • Mark success on the agreed successful response range. Retry network errors, timeouts, and selected retryable statuses with exponential backoff and jitter; honor bounded retry guidance. Cap attempts or event age, then move the record to an inspectable failed state. Do not retry every permanent 4xx indefinitely.
  • If a receiver commits and its acknowledgement is lost, the sender cannot know whether processing happened. It must retry and the receiver should deduplicate the stable event ID in the same transaction as its business update. A queue's exactly-once feature has a specific scope and does not make arbitrary HTTP effects exactly once.
  • Expose delivery attempts, next retry, and a controlled replay API. Monitor oldest backlog age, success rate, attempt amplification, per-destination latency, and failed-event count. Preserve ordering only where required; strict ordering can let one poison event block later ones.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• At-least-once delivery is recoverable but requires duplicate-tolerant consumers. At-most-once avoids retries but can lose events.
  • Per-destination ordering simplifies some consumers and reduces throughput/availability when a message fails.
  • Long retention helps recovery but consumes storage and may retain sensitive payloads; store only what the product needs.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Kill a worker after the receiver accepts but before local acknowledgement; expect a duplicate with the same ID.
  • Simulate 429, 500, a permanent 400, a hanging response, secret rotation, and an invalid registered destination.
  • Drain a large backlog without starving new traffic or unrelated tenants; replay must retain a deliberate deduplication policy.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you handle per-user ordering, schema evolution, destination deletion, and receiver-managed replay cursors?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Identifies the durable acknowledgement boundary and lease/retry policy.
  • Explains duplicate handling end to end, with correct scope for guarantees.
  • Prevents one tenant or poison event from exhausting shared resources.

cards.title: Paginate a changing activity feed
cards.question:
Design a paginated tenant activity feed that remains efficient deep into a large history while new events arrive. Explain cursor contents, ordering, permissions, and what consistency the client gets.

Requirements

  • Return up to 50 rows per page, newest first, with an opaque next-page token.
  • Support a fixed tenant and event-type filter across a traversal.
  • Define behavior for inserts and deletions during pagination; do not promise a snapshot accidentally.

Assumed scale

Assume 50 million retained rows, 2,000 list requests/s, and a target p95 under 150 ms. Rows have immutable created_at and a unique ID; many rows share the same timestamp.
cards.answer:
Define a total order (created_at DESC, id DESC). For a page after cursor (t,id), query rows whose tuple is smaller, with the same tenant/filter, ordered by the same keys, LIMIT pageSize+1. The extra row determines whether another page exists.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Choose a unique stable ordering before designing the token. A timestamp alone is not enough.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Define a total order (created_at DESC, id DESC). For a page after cursor (t,id), query rows whose tuple is smaller, with the same tenant/filter, ordered by the same keys, LIMIT pageSize+1. The extra row determines whether another page exists.
  • Use an index beginning with the equality predicates such as (tenant_id,event_type,created_at DESC,id DESC), adjusting to actual query patterns. Large OFFSET values require the database to find and skip earlier rows; keyset pagination seeks near the cursor instead.
  • Encode the last returned tuple, normalized filter/version, tenant scope, expiry, and optionally a traversal high-water mark in a signed opaque token. Validate size and version; reject changed filters. The token is a continuation mechanism, not authorization: check access on every request.
  • Choose a moving-view guarantee: new higher-ranked rows appear on refresh, not in later pages. Deletions may shorten pages. Immutable order keys avoid moving existing rows across the boundary. A first-page high-water mark can exclude later high-ranked inserts but does not provide a full snapshot when rows can be deleted or backfilled.
  • If a stable export is required, create a snapshot/materialized export job with its own lifecycle instead of holding a database transaction open across a user's long browsing session. Bound page size, token lifetime, query timeout, and allowed filters.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Keyset pagination supports efficient sequential traversal but cannot cheaply jump to arbitrary page 1,000.
  • Opaque tokens let the backend evolve; exposing raw offsets or database keys as a public contract makes migrations harder.
  • A moving feed prioritizes fresh data and low cost. Stable historical exports need stronger snapshot semantics and storage.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Use many equal timestamps, insert new rows between pages, delete the last row from a prior page, and change permissions mid-traversal.
  • Tamper with the token, change filters, use an expired token, and try a token from another tenant.
  • Measure deep-page plans and latency with realistic skew; verify no duplicate rows when immutable keys and a fixed query are used.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Add reverse pagination, full-text ranking, multi-region writes, or a legally auditable point-in-time export.

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Uses a unique order and matching seek predicate/index.
  • Binds tokens to query context while rechecking permissions.
  • States the actual consistency contract for concurrent changes.

cards.title: Prevent a hot-key cache stampede
cards.question:
A read API uses cache-aside metadata caching. When a popular key expires, thousands of requests hit the origin simultaneously. Design a recovery path that protects the origin and returns appropriately fresh data.

Requirements

  • For this exercise, metadata may be stale for at most 60 seconds after its freshness TTL; authorization decisions may not use this stale policy.
  • A failed refresh must not create an unbounded request pile-up.
  • Explain local versus fleet-wide request coalescing and data updates racing with refreshes.

Assumed scale

Assume 15,000 reads/s, an origin sustainable capacity of 2,000 reads/s, and one hot key receiving 1,000 reads/s. An origin refresh takes 200 ms, so an uncoalesced miss burst can create roughly 200 simultaneous refreshes for that one key.
cards.answer:
Store value, source version, fresh-until, and stale-until. Fresh entries return immediately. A stale-but-allowed entry returns its value while triggering a refresh. After stale-until, either wait within a short bound for a refresh or fail according to the endpoint's contract.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Separate fresh, stale-but-allowed, and unusable states. Then decide who may refresh each state and for how long.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Store value, source version, fresh-until, and stale-until. Fresh entries return immediately. A stale-but-allowed entry returns its value while triggering a refresh. After stale-until, either wait within a short bound for a refresh or fail according to the endpoint's contract.
  • Coalesce same-key refreshes within each process using a pending promise/task. For fleet-wide protection, use a bounded distributed lease or a dedicated refresh worker so many processes do not each call the origin. A lease is an optimization: its expiry may allow overlapping refreshes.
  • Write refreshed values only if their source version is at least the stored version, or use a compare-and-set rule. Otherwise a slow old refresh can overwrite a newer value. A lock alone does not solve the stale-writer problem after lease expiry.
  • Add TTL jitter to spread synchronized expirations, a global refresh concurrency cap, deadlines, and backoff after repeated failures. Jitter spreads many keys; it does not prevent one extremely hot key from stamping. Use negative caching only for explicitly safe, short-lived not-found outcomes.
  • Monitor origin QPS, refresh concurrency, hit/fresh/stale/miss rates, age served, lease contention, and refresh failures. Include tenant/permission/version context in cache keys where values differ; a fast cache must not leak another tenant's data.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Stale-while-revalidate improves availability but requires a real product freshness allowance.
  • Distributed leases reduce duplicate work but add a dependency; local coalescing is simpler and may suffice at small scale.
  • Longer TTL improves hit rate but delays visibility; invalidation/versioning adds coordination and failure cases.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Expire the hottest key under load; confirm refresh work is bounded rather than proportional to request count.
  • Crash the lease holder, delay an old refresh beyond lease expiry, and publish a newer source version during that delay.
  • Simulate origin failure until stale-until passes; verify the app stops serving data beyond its stated freshness limit.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: What changes for rapidly changing permissions, large values, a multilevel CDN/application cache, or a backend that cannot return versions?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Bounds duplicate refreshes and waiting clients.
  • States freshness limits and handles stale writers.
  • Tests overload and failures rather than assuming a good cache hit rate is sufficient.

cards.title: Ship a change with measurable reliability
cards.question:
Design a rollout and monitoring plan for a new API implementation. The dashboard shows a stable average latency, but a small group of users experiences failures and long waits. Decide what to measure and when to stop the rollout.

Requirements

  • Define a user-centered success SLI and a latency SLI with explicit denominators.
  • Roll out gradually with a fast rollback or disable path.
  • Avoid high-cardinality telemetry labels containing arbitrary user IDs, URLs, or request bodies.

Assumed scale

Assume 10 million eligible requests/day and a 99.9% successful-request SLO over 28 days. At a steady volume, 280 million requests allow about 280,000 unsuccessful requests. A 5% failure rate burns budget 50× faster than the allowed 0.1% error rate.
cards.answer:
Define eligible requests and success precisely: for example, valid authorized requests that return a correct response before the product deadline. Separate expected client errors from service failures deliberately, rather than silently removing all 4xx or timeouts from the denominator.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Start from a user's successful interaction, not CPU utilization. Identify the population your denominator excludes.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Define eligible requests and success precisely: for example, valid authorized requests that return a correct response before the product deadline. Separate expected client errors from service failures deliberately, rather than silently removing all 4xx or timeouts from the denominator.
  • Measure latency as a distribution or as the fraction below a user-relevant threshold. A mean hides tails, and averaging per-instance p99 values does not produce a global p99. Aggregate compatible histogram buckets/counts or an appropriate distribution representation.
  • Canary the change on a small, representative traffic slice; compare success, latency, resource use, and business correctness with a control. Segment using bounded dimensions such as region, client version, and endpoint class to uncover concentrated failures.
  • Set rollback triggers before release: sustained excess errors, deadline misses, saturation, or a correctness invariant violation. Use both short and longer observation windows to distinguish a short spike from persistent budget consumption. Keep a manual stop and test the rollback path.
  • Propagate request deadlines and trace context. Use metrics for fleet-wide detection, sampled traces for causality, and structured logs for specific events. Redact sensitive data and keep a release/version marker so an incident can be correlated to the change.
  • After a rollback, preserve evidence, reduce impact, and write down the failed assumption and a prevention test. A green dashboard is insufficient if the SLI excludes the affected users or the sample is too small.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• A small canary reduces blast radius but needs enough traffic and representative cohorts to reveal failures.
  • Aggressive rollback thresholds reduce damage but can react to noise; thresholds should reflect volume and business cost.
  • More tracing helps diagnosis but adds storage/overhead and privacy exposure; sampling needs a deliberate policy.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Inject a failure limited to one region or client version; ensure segmentation catches it.
  • Cause a long-tail latency regression while holding the mean steady, and simulate missing telemetry.
  • Exercise rollback with a backward-compatible data/schema migration; verify older code can still serve safely.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: How would you handle low-traffic services, asynchronous workflows, schema changes that cannot be rolled back, or an SLO that conflicts with cost?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Defines measurable SLIs and calculates budget consumption correctly.
  • Distinguishes detection, diagnosis, and mitigation.
  • Connects rollout decisions to user impact and validates rollback compatibility.

cards.title: Reserve scarce inventory without overselling
cards.question:
Design a reservation API for a limited-capacity workshop. Multiple clients may reserve the last seat at the same time; clients retry and abandoned reservations expire.

Requirements

  • Never confirm more seats than capacity. A user cannot hold duplicate active reservations for the same workshop.
  • Reservation creation is retry-safe and holds expire after 10 minutes unless confirmed.
  • Explain which state changes must be atomic and how confirmation races with expiry.

Assumed scale

Assume 2 million workshops, usually under 100 seats each. Normal traffic is 300 reservation requests/s, but a popular workshop can receive 5,000 requests/s for its last few seats. Most contention is concentrated on one row/key.
cards.answer:
Choose one authoritative database transaction for the capacity invariant. A simple model locks the workshop row, checks remaining capacity, inserts a reservation with a unique business/idempotency key, and decrements remaining seats atomically. An atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE remaining > 0 is another valid foundation.

Treat these numbers and choices as exercise assumptions. A strong answer states the consistency guarantee, walks through one request and one failure, and explains a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Hint
sections.html: Write the invariant and the legal state transitions before selecting databases. Find the smallest atomic boundary that preserves them.

sections.title: Worked walkthrough
sections.html:
• Choose one authoritative database transaction for the capacity invariant. A simple model locks the workshop row, checks remaining capacity, inserts a reservation with a unique business/idempotency key, and decrements remaining seats atomically. An atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE remaining > 0 is another valid foundation.
  • Store reservations with an explicit state such as HELD, CONFIRMED, EXPIRED, or CANCELLED, plus expires_at and an idempotency key. Enforce duplicate-active-reservation policy with an appropriate database constraint or a separate unique active-ownership row; application pre-checks alone race.
  • Confirm using a conditional state transition that verifies HELD and an unexpired deadline under the same lock/transaction policy. The expiry worker similarly changes HELD to EXPIRED and releases capacity exactly once. Whichever valid transition wins prevents the other from also releasing or confirming the seat.
  • A periodic expiry worker is not a precise timer. The confirmation path must check expiry itself, and reservation creation may reclaim expired holds transactionally if the product needs immediate reuse. Use the authoritative database time for these decisions.
  • Handle transaction serialization/deadlock failures with bounded retries and the same operation identity. Do not perform slow external calls while holding the hot row lock. Emit confirmation notifications through an outbox so notification failure does not roll back an already committed reservation.
  • Scale hot workshops by limiting admission/queueing contention before the database and making rejection fast. Sharding helps independent workshops; splitting one capacity invariant across shards requires quota allocation or stronger coordination, not just adding replicas.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.html:
• Pessimistic locking gives a clear invariant but serializes a hot workshop. Optimistic compare-and-swap may retry heavily under contention.
  • Long holds are user-friendly but reduce availability of scarce seats; short holds need clear expiry UX.
  • Read replicas can serve browsing availability approximately, but final reservation decisions must use the authoritative transaction.

sections.title: Failure cases and tests
sections.html:
• Race 100 clients for one seat; exactly one hold succeeds and capacity never becomes negative.
  • Race confirmation with expiry, retry a committed reservation after a lost response, and replay the expiry job.
  • Kill workers after committing a state change, inject transaction conflicts, and verify the capacity plus held/confirmed-count invariant.

sections.title: Interviewer follow-up
sections.html: Add multi-seat reservations, cancellation, waitlists, or reservations spanning two workshops. Which operations introduce multi-resource transactions?

sections.title: Self-review rubric
sections.html:
• Protects capacity and uniqueness with database-enforced atomicity.
  • Handles expiry/confirmation and retry races without double release.
  • Explains hot-key contention and the actual consistency requirements.

Keep a map from each previously visited value to its index. Look up the current value’s complement before inserting the current index, which prevents using one position twice.

cards.title: Add Two Numbers
cards.summary: Add two nonnegative integers represented by linked lists of decimal digits in least-significant-first order.
cards.question:
Add two nonnegative integers represented by linked lists of decimal digits in least-significant-first order.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Advance through both lists while carrying the tens part of each digit sum. Continue until both lists and the carry are exhausted, emitting each remainder digit into a new list.

Target complexity

O(max(m,n)) time and output space; O(1) working state, without converting whole numbers to machine integers.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • 0 plus 0 → one zero node
  • 9→9 plus 1 → 0→0→1
  • Unequal list lengths preserve the longer remainder

sections.title: How to approach it
sections.html: Advance through both lists while carrying the tens part of each digit sum. Continue until both lists and the carry are exhausted, emitting each remainder digit into a new list.

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0002.Add%20Two%20Numbers/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(
        self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]
    ) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode()
        carry, curr = 0, dummy
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            s = (l1.val if l1 else 0) + (l2.val if l2 else 0) + carry
            carry, val = divmod(s, 10)
            curr.next = ListNode(val)
            curr = curr.next
            l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
            l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
        return dummy.next

Keep one buffer per row and a direction flag. Append each character to the current row, reversing direction only at the first or last row; concatenate the buffers at the end.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

  • One row: preserve the input.
  • More rows than characters: no rearrangement.
  • Two rows: alternate between them.

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0019.Remove%20Nth%20Node%20From%20End%20of%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        fast = slow = dummy
        for _ in range(n):
            fast = fast.next
        while fast.next:
            slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
        slow.next = slow.next.next
        return dummy.next

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0023.Merge%20k%20Sorted%20Lists/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        setattr(ListNode, "__lt__", lambda a, b: a.val < b.val)
        pq = [head for head in lists if head]
        heapify(pq)
        dummy = cur = ListNode()
        while pq:
            node = heappop(pq)
            if node.next:
                heappush(pq, node.next)
            cur.next = node
            cur = cur.next
        return dummy.next

# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0024.Swap%20Nodes%20in%20Pairs/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head
        t = self.swapPairs(head.next.next)
        p = head.next
        p.next = head
        head.next = t
        return p

cards.summary: Reverse each complete block of k nodes in a linked list, leaving a shorter final block in its original order.
cards.question:
Reverse each complete block of k nodes in a linked list, leaving a shorter final block in its original order.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Before changing links, find the kth node to confirm the whole block exists. Reverse the block toward the following node, reconnect its new head, and use its old head as the predecessor for the next block.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(1) space; values remain unchanged and only links are rewired.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • k=1 leaves the list unchanged
  • Five nodes with k=2 leave the last node unchanged
  • k equal to list length reverses the entire list

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0025.Reverse%20Nodes%20in%20k-Group/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        def reverse(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
            dummy = ListNode()
            cur = head
            while cur:
                nxt = cur.next
                cur.next = dummy.next
                dummy.next = cur
                cur = nxt
            return dummy.next

        dummy = pre = ListNode(next=head)
        while pre:
            cur = pre
            for _ in range(k):
                cur = cur.next
                if cur is None:
                    return dummy.next
            node = pre.next
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = None
            pre.next = reverse(node)
            node.next = nxt
            pre = node
        return dummy.next

Build a prefix-failure table for the pattern, then scan the text with a pattern pointer. On a mismatch, retain the longest usable matched prefix instead of moving the text pointer backward; the first complete match is the answer.

cards.question:
Find starting positions where a contiguous region consists of exactly the supplied equal-length words, in any order.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Build the required word-frequency map and scan separately for every offset modulo the word length. Extend by one word at a time, clearing on an unknown word and shrinking when a word is overrepresented; record windows containing the required total number of words.

Target complexity

With n text characters, word length w, and k words: O(nw + kw) time if slicing/hashing each token costs O(w); O(kw) key storage. Token operations can reduce the scan to O(n).

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • The word list contains duplicate words.
  • Several valid windows overlap.
  • The full concatenation is longer than the text.

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0030.Substring%20with%20Concatenation%20of%20All%20Words/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def findSubstring(self, s: str, words: List[str]) -> List[int]:
        cnt = Counter(words)
        m, n = len(s), len(words)
        k = len(words[0])
        ans = []
        for i in range(k):
            l = r = i
            cnt1 = Counter()
            while r + k <= m:
                t = s[r : r + k]
                r += k
                if cnt[t] == 0:
                    l = r
                    cnt1.clear()
                    continue
                cnt1[t] += 1
                while cnt1[t] > cnt[t]:
                    rem = s[l : l + k]
                    l += k
                    cnt1[rem] -= 1
                if r - l == n * k:
                    ans.append(l)
        return ans

cards.question:
Transform an array into its next lexicographic permutation, wrapping to the smallest arrangement when necessary.

Find the rightmost position whose value is smaller than its successor. Swap it with the rightmost larger suffix value, then reverse the suffix, which was nonincreasing; if there is no pivot, reverse the whole array.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(1) extra space with in-place reversal.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • A fully descending array wraps around.
  • Repeated values require a strictly larger swap.
  • A one-element array is unchanged.

class Solution:
    def searchRange(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
        l = bisect_left(nums, target)

Backtrack in nondecreasing candidate-index order to avoid producing different permutations of the same combination. Taking a candidate keeps its index available; skipping it moves forward, and a sum above the target ends the branch.

  • [2], target 1 → no combinations
  • [2], target 6 → [[2,2,2]]
  • [2,3,6,7], target 7 → [2,2,3] and [7]

# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0047.Permutations%20II/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def permuteUnique(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        def dfs(i: int):
            if i == n:
                ans.append(t[:])
                return
            for j in range(n):
                if vis[j] or (j and nums[j] == nums[j - 1] and not vis[j - 1]):
                    continue
                t[i] = nums[j]
                vis[j] = True
                dfs(i + 1)
                vis[j] = False

        n = len(nums)
        nums.sort()
        ans = []
        t = [0] * n
        vis = [False] * n
        dfs(0)
        return ans

cards.question:
Place n queens on an n×n chessboard so none share a row, column, or diagonal, returning every valid board.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Place one queen per row and track occupied columns and the two diagonal identifiers row+column and row-column. Undo all three markings when backtracking, and copy the board only after all rows are placed.

Target complexity

Exponential search; a safe O(n·n! + S·n²) bound includes scanning columns and copying S boards. O(n²) board plus O(n) search state, excluding output.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

  • n=1 has one board
  • n=2 and n=3 have no solutions
  • n=4 has two boards

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0051.N-Queens/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        def dfs(i: int):
            if i == n:
                ans.append(["".join(row) for row in g])
                return
            for j in range(n):
                if col[j] + dg[i + j] + udg[n - i + j] == 0:
                    g[i][j] = "Q"
                    col[j] = dg[i + j] = udg[n - i + j] = 1
                    dfs(i + 1)
                    col[j] = dg[i + j] = udg[n - i + j] = 0
                    g[i][j] = "."

        ans = []
        g = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]
        col = [0] * n
        dg = [0] * (n << 1)
        udg = [0] * (n << 1)
        dfs(0)
        return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0052.N-Queens%20II/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def totalNQueens(self, n: int) -> int:
        def dfs(i: int):
            if i == n:
                nonlocal ans
                ans += 1
                return
            for j in range(n):
                a, b = i + j, i - j + n
                if cols[j] or dg[a] or udg[b]:
                    continue
                cols[j] = dg[a] = udg[b] = True
                dfs(i + 1)
                cols[j] = dg[a] = udg[b] = False

        cols = [False] * 10
        dg = [False] * 20
        udg = [False] * 20
        ans = 0
        dfs(0)
        return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0054.Spiral%20Matrix/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        dirs = (0, 1, 0, -1, 0)
        vis = [[False] * n for _ in range(m)]
        i = j = k = 0
        ans = []
        for _ in range(m * n):
            ans.append(matrix[i][j])
            vis[i][j] = True
            x, y = i + dirs[k], j + dirs[k + 1]
            if x < 0 or x >= m or y < 0 or y >= n or vis[x][y]:
                k = (k + 1) % 4
            i += dirs[k]
            j += dirs[k + 1]
        return ans

cards.title: Rotate List
cards.summary: Rotate a linked list to the right by k positions while reusing its nodes.
cards.question:
Rotate a linked list to the right by k positions while reusing its nodes.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Find the list length and reduce k modulo that length. Locate the new tail n-k nodes from the start, join the old tail to the old head, and cut the link after the new tail to restore a linear list.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(1) extra space; remember to break the temporary cycle.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • An empty list must avoid modulo by zero.
  • k is a multiple of the list length.
  • k is much larger than the list length.

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0061.Rotate%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head
        cur, n = head, 0
        while cur:
            n += 1
            cur = cur.next
        k %= n
        if k == 0:
            return head
        fast = slow = head
        for _ in range(k):
            fast = fast.next
        while fast.next:
            fast, slow = fast.next, slow.next

        ans = slow.next
        slow.next = None
        fast.next = head
        return ans

cards.question:

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.

How to approach it

Greedily take the largest group of words that fits with at least one space between neighbors. For ordinary lines, divide spare spaces among gaps and give the remainder to earlier gaps; a last line or a single-word line is left-aligned and padded on the right.

Target complexity

O(total output characters) construction time with buffers, plus scanning the input; output storage is proportional to the padded lines.

  • A line contains only one word.
  • Extra spaces do not divide evenly across gaps.
  • The final line fits fewer words than earlier lines.

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0068.Text%20Justification/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def fullJustify(self, words: List[str], maxWidth: int) -> List[str]:
        ans = []
        i, n = 0, len(words)
        while i < n:
            t = []
            cnt = len(words[i])
            t.append(words[i])
            i += 1
            while i < n and cnt + 1 + len(words[i]) <= maxWidth:
                cnt += 1 + len(words[i])
                t.append(words[i])
                i += 1
            if i == n or len(t) == 1:
                left = ' '.join(t)
                right = ' ' * (maxWidth - len(left))
                ans.append(left + right)
                continue
            space_width = maxWidth - (cnt - len(t) + 1)
            w, m = divmod(space_width, len(t) - 1)
            row = []
            for j, s in enumerate(t[:-1]):
                row.append(s)
                row.append(' ' * (w + (1 if j < m else 0)))
            row.append(t[-1])
            ans.append(''.join(row))
        return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0077.Combinations/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def combine(self, n: int, k: int) -> List[List[int]]:
        def dfs(i: int):
            if len(t) == k:
                ans.append(t[:])
                return
            if i > n:
                return
            t.append(i)
            dfs(i + 1)
            t.pop()
            dfs(i + 1)

        ans = []
        t = []
        dfs(1)
        return ans

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0086.Partition%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def partition(self, head: Optional[ListNode], x: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        l = ListNode()
        r = ListNode()
        tl, tr = l, r
        while head:
            if head.val < x:
                tl.next = head
                tl = tl.next
            else:
                tr.next = head
                tr = tr.next
            head = head.next
        tr.next = None
        tl.next = r.next
        return l.next

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0000-0099/0090.Subsets%20II/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def subsetsWithDup(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        def dfs(i: int):
            if i == len(nums):
                ans.append(t[:])
                return
            t.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            x = t.pop()
            while i + 1 < len(nums) and nums[i + 1] == x:
                i += 1
            dfs(i + 1)

        nums.sort()
        ans = []
        t = []
        dfs(0)
        return ans

#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reverseBetween(
        self, head: Optional[ListNode], left: int, right: int
    ) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if head.next is None or left == right:
            return head
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        pre = dummy
        for _ in range(left - 1):
            pre = pre.next
        p, q = pre, pre.next
        cur = q
        for _ in range(right - left + 1):
            t = cur.next
            cur.next = pre
            pre, cur = cur, t
        p.next = pre
        q.next = cur
        return dummy.next

#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left

class Solution:
    def inorderTraversal(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:

            dfs(root.left)

            dfs(root.right)

        dfs(root)

#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):

#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        ans = []
        if root is None:
            return ans
        q = deque([root])
        while q:
            t = []
            for _ in range(len(q)):
                node = q.popleft()
                t.append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    q.append(node.left)
                if node.right:
                    q.append(node.right)
            ans.append(t)
        return ans

#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def zigzagLevelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        ans = []
        if root is None:
            return ans
        q = deque([root])
        ans = []
        left = 1
        while q:
            t = []
            for _ in range(len(q)):
                node = q.popleft()
                t.append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    q.append(node.left)
                if node.right:
                    q.append(node.right)
            ans.append(t if left else t[::-1])
            left ^= 1
        return ans

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0114.Flatten%20Binary%20Tree%20to%20Linked%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def flatten(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> None:
        """
        Do not return anything, modify root in-place instead.
        """
        while root:
            if root.left:
                pre = root.left
                while pre.right:
                    pre = pre.right
                pre.right = root.right
                root.right = root.left
                root.left = None
            root = root.right

cards.question:

cards.answer:
How to approach it

For each pair of source and target indices, always allow skipping the source character. When the characters match, also count taking it; an exhausted target contributes one completed choice, while an exhausted source with target remaining contributes zero.

Target complexity

O(mn) time and O(mn) space, reducible to O(n) by updating target indices backward. Generalized counts can require arbitrary-precision integers.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • "aaa" → "aa" has 3 choices
  • A target longer than the source has 0 choices
  • Identical nonrepeating strings have 1 choice

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0123.Best%20Time%20to%20Buy%20and%20Sell%20Stock%20III/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def maxProfit(self, prices: List[int]) -> int:
        # 第一次买入，第一次卖出，第二次买入，第二次卖出
        f1, f2, f3, f4 = -prices[0], 0, -prices[0], 0
        for price in prices[1:]:
            f1 = max(f1, -price)
            f2 = max(f2, f1 + price)
            f3 = max(f3, f2 - price)
            f4 = max(f4, f3 + price)
        return f4

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0124.Binary%20Tree%20Maximum%20Path%20Sum/Solution.py

# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def maxPathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        def dfs(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
            if root is None:
                return 0
            left = max(0, dfs(root.left))
            right = max(0, dfs(root.right))
            nonlocal ans
            ans = max(ans, root.val + left + right)
            return root.val + max(left, right)

        ans = -inf
        dfs(root)
        return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0128.Longest%20Consecutive%20Sequence/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def longestConsecutive(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        s = set(nums)
        ans = 0
        d = defaultdict(int)
        for x in nums:
            y = x
            while y in s:
                s.remove(y)
                y += 1
            d[x] = d[y] + y - x
            ans = max(ans, d[x])
        return ans

From the current start index, try each endpoint whose substring is a palindrome and recurse on the remaining suffix. Record the current list of pieces when the entire string has been consumed; a precomputed palindrome table avoids repeated checks.

Target complexity

Exponential output, up to O(n·2^n) output characters. Palindrome-table preprocessing costs O(n²); repeated scans and slicing can add overhead.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • "a" → [["a"]]
  • "aab" → ["a","a","b"] and ["aa","b"]
  • "aaa" has four valid partitions

cards.title: Gas Station
cards.summary: Find a starting station that permits a full circular trip using each station’s gas and each outgoing leg’s cost, or report impossibility.
cards.question:
Find a starting station that permits a full circular trip using each station’s gas and each outgoing leg’s cost, or report impossibility.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

The total gas must cover the total cost. In a forward scan, whenever the running tank becomes negative, discard every start in that failed segment and restart immediately after it; the surviving start works when the total balance is nonnegative.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(1) space; the total-balance check is necessary for the reset-on-deficit strategy.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • One station with gas below cost → -1
  • Equal gas and cost at the only station → 0
  • A valid start can occur after a long initial deficit

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0134.Gas%20Station/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: List[int], cost: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(gas)
        i = j = n - 1
        cnt = s = 0
        while cnt < n:
            s += gas[j] - cost[j]
            cnt += 1
            j = (j + 1) % n
            while s < 0 and cnt < n:
                i -= 1
                s += gas[i] - cost[i]
                cnt += 1
        return -1 if s < 0 else i

cards.question:
Assign the fewest rewards so every child receives one and each child with a higher rating than a neighbor receives more than that neighbor.

How to approach it

Initialize everyone to one, then scan left to right to satisfy rising comparisons with the left neighbor. Scan right to left to enforce the opposite constraint using the maximum of the existing assignment and the required right-neighbor value.

cards.question:
Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes have both next and arbitrary random pointers.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Create one fresh node for every original node and store an original-to-copy map. In a second pass, translate both pointers through that map so aliases, cycles through random links, and null links are preserved without referencing originals.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(n) mapping space plus O(n) copied nodes; interleaving nodes is an optional O(1)-auxiliary alternative.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • A node whose random pointer targets itself
  • Several nodes sharing one random target
  • Empty list → empty copy

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0138.Copy%20List%20with%20Random%20Pointer/Solution.py

"""
# Definition for a Node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, x: int, next: 'Node' = None, random: 'Node' = None):
        self.val = int(x)
        self.next = next
        self.random = random
"""


class Solution:
    def copyRandomList(self, head: "Optional[Node]") -> "Optional[Node]":
        d = {}
        dummy = tail = Node(0)
        cur = head
        while cur:
            node = Node(cur.val)
            tail.next = node
            tail = tail.next
            d[cur] = node
            cur = cur.next
        cur = head
        while cur:
            d[cur].random = d[cur.random] if cur.random else None
            cur = cur.next
        return dummy.next

Use suffix indices as subproblems and explore dictionary matches starting at each index. Memoize the possible suffix completions or first compute feasible suffixes to prune dead ends, then join words only when constructing an answer.

class Solution:
    def hasCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
        s = set()
        while head:
            if head in s:
                return True
            s.add(head)
            head = head.next
        return False

#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.next = None


class Solution:
    def detectCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        fast = slow = head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
            if slow == fast:
                ans = head
                while ans != slow:
                    ans = ans.next
                    slow = slow.next
                return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0143.Reorder%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        fast = slow = head
        while fast.next and fast.next.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        cur = slow.next
        slow.next = None

        pre = None
        while cur:
            t = cur.next
            cur.next = pre
            pre, cur = cur, t
        cur = head

        while pre:
            t = pre.next
            pre.next = cur.next
            cur.next = pre
            cur, pre = pre.next, t

#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def preorderTraversal(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
        def dfs(root):
            if root is None:
                return
            ans.append(root.val)
            dfs(root.left)
            dfs(root.right)

        ans = []
        dfs(root)
        return ans

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0146.LRU%20Cache/Solution.py

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key: int = 0, val: int = 0):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.size = 0
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = {}
        self.head = Node()
        self.tail = Node()
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        node = self.cache[key]
        self.remove_node(node)
        self.add_to_head(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.cache:
            node = self.cache[key]
            self.remove_node(node)
            node.val = value
            self.add_to_head(node)
        else:
            node = Node(key, value)
            self.cache[key] = node
            self.add_to_head(node)
            self.size += 1
            if self.size > self.capacity:
                node = self.tail.prev
                self.cache.pop(node.key)
                self.remove_node(node)
                self.size -= 1

    def remove_node(self, node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def add_to_head(self, node):
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next = node
        node.next.prev = node


# Your LRUCache object will be instantiated and called as such:
# obj = LRUCache(capacity)
# param_1 = obj.get(key)
# obj.put(key,value)

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0148.Sort%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head
        slow, fast = head, head.next
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        l1, l2 = head, slow.next
        slow.next = None
        l1, l2 = self.sortList(l1), self.sortList(l2)
        dummy = ListNode()
        tail = dummy
        while l1 and l2:
            if l1.val <= l2.val:
                tail.next = l1
                l1 = l1.next
            else:
                tail.next = l2
                l2 = l2.next
            tail = tail.next
        tail.next = l1 or l2
        return dummy.next

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0149.Max%20Points%20on%20a%20Line/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def maxPoints(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(points)
        ans = 1
        for i in range(n):
            x1, y1 = points[i]
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                x2, y2 = points[j]
                cnt = 2
                for k in range(j + 1, n):
                    x3, y3 = points[k]
                    a = (y2 - y1) * (x3 - x1)
                    b = (y3 - y1) * (x2 - x1)
                    cnt += a == b
                ans = max(ans, cnt)
        return ans

cards.summary: Find the largest product of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
cards.question:
Find the largest product of any nonempty contiguous subarray.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Track both the largest and smallest products ending at the current position. A negative value can swap their roles, while choosing the current value alone naturally restarts the subarray after a zero or an unfavorable prefix.

Target complexity

O(n) time and O(1) space; update both extrema from the previous state, not partially updated values.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

  • [-2,0,-1] → 0
  • [-2,3,-4] → 24

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0152.Maximum%20Product%20Subarray/Solution.py

class Solution:
    def maxProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        ans = f = g = nums[0]
        for x in nums[1:]:
            ff, gg = f, g
            f = max(x, ff * x, gg * x)
            g = min(x, ff * x, gg * x)
            ans = max(ans, f)
        return ans

cards.question:

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Store the minimum-so-far alongside each pushed value, either in a parallel stack or in each stack entry. Pop the value and its recorded minimum together so duplicate minima and earlier minima are restored correctly.

Target complexity

O(1) per query and amortized O(1) array push/pop; O(n) storage. Nonempty-stack calls are guaranteed by the problem.

  • Push 2,1,1; pop once → minimum 1
  • Push -2,0,-3; pop → minimum -2
  • One value serves as both top and minimum

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0155.Min%20Stack/Solution.py

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stk1 = []
        self.stk2 = [inf]

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.stk1.append(val)
        self.stk2.append(min(val, self.stk2[-1]))

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stk1.pop()
        self.stk2.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stk1[-1]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.stk2[-1]


# Your MinStack object will be instantiated and called as such:
# obj = MinStack()
# obj.push(val)

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0160.Intersection%20of%20Two%20Linked%20Lists/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.next = None


class Solution:
    def getIntersectionNode(self, headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        a, b = headA, headB
        while a != b:
            a = a.next if a else headB
            b = b.next if b else headA
        return a

Each trailing zero needs a factor pair of two and five, and factors of five are scarcer. Add the counts of multiples of 5, 25, 125, and so on, since higher powers contribute additional fives.

Target complexity

O(log5 n) time and O(1) space; repeated integer division avoids overflow when generating powers of five.

  • n below 5 contributes no zeros.
  • n = 25 includes an extra contribution from 25.
  • n = 0 uses 0! = 1.

cards.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
cards.summary: Expose a search tree’s values through an iterator that returns the next smallest value on demand.
cards.question:
Expose a search tree’s values through an iterator that returns the next smallest value on demand.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Keep the leftmost unvisited path on a stack. Pop one node for next, then push the leftmost path from its right child; the stack top always represents the next inorder value.

Target complexity

O(h) initialization and storage; next is O(h) worst-case but O(1) amortized over a full traversal, and hasNext is O(1).

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • The tree contains only one node.
  • A left-heavy tree makes initialization deep.
  • hasNext becomes false immediately after the final value.

# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0100-0199/0173.Binary%20Search%20Tree%20Iterator/Solution.py

# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class BSTIterator:
    def __init__(self, root: TreeNode):
        def inorder(root):
            if root:
                inorder(root.left)
                self.vals.append(root.val)
                inorder(root.right)

        self.cur = 0
        self.vals = []
        inorder(root)

    def next(self) -> int:
        res = self.vals[self.cur]
        self.cur += 1
        return res

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        return self.cur < len(self.vals)


# Your BSTIterator object will be instantiated and called as such:
# obj = BSTIterator(root)
# param_1 = obj.next()
# param_2 = obj.hasNext()

python.code:
# Doocs contributors · CC-BY-SA-4.0
# Source: https://github.com/doocs/leetcode/blob/88c8c2c29f19c186d7cc05c9db17245d9ae3df43/solution/0200-0299/0206.Reverse%20Linked%20List/Solution.py

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode()
        curr = head
        while curr:
            next = curr.next
            curr.next = dummy.next
            dummy.next = curr
            curr = next
        return dummy.next

cards.question:
Return the kth largest array value, counting repeated values as separate ranks.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.

How to approach it

Use a min heap of the largest k values, or partition around a pivot and recurse only into the partition containing the desired rank. Quickselect avoids fully sorting the array, but its guarantees depend on pivot selection and partition implementation.

Size-k heap: O(n log k) time/O(k) space. Randomized in-place quickselect: expected O(n), worst O(n²); out-of-place partition variants allocate extra arrays.

cards.title: Combination Sum III
cards.summary: Choose exactly k distinct digits from 1 through 9 whose total reaches a target.
cards.question:
Choose exactly k distinct digits from 1 through 9 whose total reaches a target.

Independent study brief. Open the official problem for the complete constraints and judge examples.
cards.answer:
How to approach it

Backtrack in increasing digit order so each combination is generated once. Carry the remaining count and sum, and prune when the smallest or largest possible remaining digits cannot reach that sum.

Target complexity

O(2^9 × k) is a safe fixed-domain bound including result copies; recursion uses O(k), excluding output.

These bounds describe the target approach above. Compare the reference implementation’s data structures and copying costs before assigning it the same bounds.

Cases to walk through

  • The target is too small for k distinct digits.
  • k = 9 leaves only the full set as a candidate.
  • A sum is possible only by repeating a digit, which is forbidden.

Let each DP value represent the largest square ending at that cell. A one-valued cell extends the minimum of its upper, left, and upper-left neighbors; a zero-valued cell resets the size to zero, and the largest side length is squared for the answer.
